analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish their negotiated prices and give patients a cost-lookup tool.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee from May 2021 until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written price-disclosure rules directly into federal health law. Hospitals would have to publish, in plain language and machine-readable form, their list prices, the rates they negotiated with each insurer, their discounted cash prices, and billing codes, plus pricing for at least 300 services patients can schedule in advance. Health insurance plans would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates, the negotiated prices of prescription drugs, and give patients a free online tool to look up what a specific service would cost them. Codifying these requirements in statute would have made them harder for a future administration to weaken or repeal than rules created by executive-branch regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone paying for health care. Today the rates a hospital negotiates with each insurer are confidential, so patients cannot compare prices before scheduling care. The bill would have forced hospitals and insurers to publish those rates, cash prices, and drug prices, and to provide a free search tool showing an individual's estimated out-of-pocket cost before care is delivered. Employers buying coverage and independent researchers would also gain visibility into what care really costs.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish their chargemaster prices, payer-specific negotiated rates, de-identified minimum and maximum negotiated rates, and discounted cash prices, in plain language, free of charge, in a consumer-friendly machine-readable format [S3].

Hospitals must disclose pricing for at least 300 shoppable services, or provide a free internet price-estimator tool covering at least 300 services that shows consumers their estimated out-of-pocket cost without requiring personal information [S3].

Insurance plans must publish in-network rates, out-of-network allowed amounts and billed charges, and negotiated rates and historical net prices for prescription drugs, including rebates and discounts the insurer receives [S3].

Plans must provide a free, subscription-free online tool giving real-time estimates of an individual's cost-sharing for a covered item or service, searchable by provider and sortable by geography and cost, plus a paper option on request [S3].
The requirements would apply to group health plans, including self-insured plans, not just individual-market qualified health plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers would bear the cost of compiling and publishing their negotiated rates, building and maintaining the price-estimator tools, and potentially a civil monetary penalty of up to $300 per day for ongoing noncompliance [S3]. Hospitals and insurers argue those compliance costs and the exposure of negotiated rates would push back on their pricing power; some of that cost could be passed to patients through premiums.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement penalty is capped at $300 per day of ongoing violation [S3] — roughly $110,000 a year, a small sum for a large hospital system, so the statutory penalty alone would give regulators little leverage compared to the value of keeping negotiated rates confidential.

Compliance is a real cost: publishing prices for at least 300 shoppable services and maintaining a real-time, personalized cost-estimator tool imposes ongoing technical and administrative burdens, which fall hardest on smaller hospitals [S3].

Transparency by itself does not lower prices: publishing rates lets patients compare, but most patients in an emergency or within a narrow insurance network have little ability to shop, and disclosure of negotiated rates can also erode the discounts some hospitals give self-pay patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and durable: written into statute, hospital and insurer price disclosure would let patients, employers, and researchers see what care actually costs, and it could not be quietly repealed by a future administration the way an executive-branch rule can. The weaknesses are a maximum penalty of $300 per day, which is small relative to what hospitals gain from confidential pricing, and the fact that transparency helps most where patients can plan care in advance rather than in emergencies. A serious version would pair the disclosure mandate with stronger penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in May 2021, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson introduced the Health Care PRICE Transparency Act on May 7, 2021, with five original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On May 10, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
The bill gathered 6 cosponsors, all Republicans, and took no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers were better off because the bill died: their negotiated rates, cash prices, and drug-rebate arrangements were never put under a statutory disclosure requirement that future administrations could not unwind. Patients never gained the statutory right to see a price before scheduling care.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the House never recorded where members stood; the bill's sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Republicans, and it died in committee without Democratic action either for or against it [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced hospitals to publish their chargemaster prices, the rates negotiated with each insurer, discounted cash prices, and pricing for at least 300 schedulable services, with a penalty of up to $300 per day for noncompliance. Confidential negotiated rates are a core part of hospital pricing power, so hospitals resisted the mandate; patients pay more when they cannot see prices in advance.

Plans would have had to publish in-network and out-of-network rates, prescription drug prices including rebates, and build a free real-time cost-estimator tool for members, and the mandate would cover employer and self-insured plans too. Insurers' negotiated rates are commercially sensitive; disclosure shifts bargaining leverage to patients and employers.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug rebate intermediaries
industries.note: The bill would have required insurers to disclose the historical net price of drugs, allocating rebates, discounts, and fees the insurer receives. That would pull back the curtain on the rebate system that keeps list prices high and obscures what patients' plans really pay.
